lead: A relation is a set of ordered pairs. It records which elements of one set are linked to which elements of another. Because it is a set, every question about a relation becomes a membership question: is this pair in or out? Two pictures make membership easy to see. A 0-1 matrix marks each allowed pair with 1 or 0. A directed graph draws each pair as an arrow. These views turn reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity into simple checks on a grid or a diagram. Database tables and graph models use the same idea.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.1 for subsets of A × B and ordered pairs.

sections.h3: A relation is a subset of A × B

blocks.text: A binary relation R from set A to set B is a subset of the Cartesian product A × B. Write (a,b) ∈ R when a is related to b, and a R b as shorthand. The domain is {a ∈ A : (a,b) ∈ R for some b ∈ B}. The range is {b ∈ B : (a,b) ∈ R for some a ∈ A}. The codomain is B, the full target set. A relation on A is a subset of A × A. An n-ary relation is a subset of A₁ × ... × Aₙ; this chapter uses binary relations only.
The inverse relation reverses every pair: R⁻¹ = {(b,a) : (a,b) ∈ R}. The complement relation uses the rest of A × B: R̄ = (A × B) − R.

blocks.where: R is a relation from A to B; R⁻¹ is the inverse relation from B to A.

blocks.text: The 0-1 matrix has one row per element of A and one column per element of B. Entry mᵢⱼ = 1 if (aᵢ,bⱼ) ∈ R, else 0. The directed graph, or digraph, has a vertex for each element and an arrow a→b for each pair (a,b) ∈ R; a pair (a,a) is a loop. Some syllabi call the matrix the adjacency matrix or connection matrix.

sections.h3: Properties read from matrix and diagram

blocks.text: Let R be a relation on a finite set A with n elements. The matrix tests use the main diagonal, the entries at row i, column i.

items: Reflexive: (a,a) ∈ R for every a ∈ A. Matrix: whole main diagonal is 1. Digraph: loop at every vertex.
Irreflexive: no (a,a) is in R. Matrix: main diagonal all 0. Digraph: no loops.
Symmetric: if (a,b) ∈ R then (b,a) ∈ R. Matrix equals its transpose: mᵢⱼ = mⱼᵢ. Digraph: every arrow has a partner back; a loop is its own partner.
Antisymmetric: if (a,b) ∈ R and (b,a) ∈ R then a = b. Matrix: no pair of opposite 1s off the diagonal. Digraph: no two distinct vertices point at each other.
Asymmetric: if (a,b) ∈ R then (b,a) ∉ R. Matrix: no opposite pair, and diagonal all 0. Digraph: no loops and no two-way arrows.
Transitive: if (a,b) ∈ R and (b,c) ∈ R then (a,c) ∈ R. Matrix: the Boolean square M² has no 1 where M has 0, written M² ≤ M entrywise. Digraph: every two-step path has a one-step shortcut.

blocks.text: On an n-element set there are 2^(n²) relations, because A × A has n² pairs and each is in or out. Reflexive relations fix all n diagonal pairs, so there are 2^(n²−n). Symmetric relations choose the diagonal and one triangle freely, so there are 2^(n(n+1)/2).
Union and intersection act pair by pair: R ∪ S and R ∩ S are ordinary set operations on the ordered pairs. The complement is relative to A × B.
S ∘ R = {(a,c) : there exists b ∈ B with (a,b) ∈ R and (b,c) ∈ S}
blocks.where: R is from A to B; S is from B to C; b runs over B; apply R first, then S.

blocks.text: In matrices, S ∘ R is the Boolean product of M_R and M_S. A function from A to B is a relation in which every a ∈ A appears in exactly one pair. Functions get their own treatment in Chapter 2.6.

figure.caption: The relation R = {(1,1),(1,2),(2,3),(3,3)} as a digraph. The arrows 1→2 and 2→3 demand 1→3; that arrow is absent, so R is not transitive.

spec.aria: A digraph on vertices 1, 2, 3 with loops at 1 and 3 and arrows 1 to 2 and 2 to 3.

examples.question: Let A = {1,2,3} and R = {(1,1),(1,2),(2,3),(3,3)}. (a) Test reflexivity, symmetry, antisymmetry and transitivity. (b) Write the 0-1 matrix and draw the digraph. (c) Find R⁻¹ and R ∘ R.
steps: Reflexive test: (1,1) ∈ R yes, (2,2) ∈ R no, (3,3) ∈ R yes. One missing diagonal pair is enough, so R is not reflexive.
Symmetric test: (1,2) ∈ R but (2,1) ∉ R. So R is not symmetric.
Antisymmetric test: the off-diagonal 1s are (1,2) and (2,3). Their reverses (2,1) and (3,2) are absent. No two distinct elements point at each other, so R is antisymmetric.
Transitive test: (1,2) ∈ R and (2,3) ∈ R, but (1,3) ∉ R. So R is not transitive.
Matrix rows for elements 1,2,3: row 1 is [1,1,0], row 2 is [0,0,1], row 3 is [0,0,1]. Row-major entries are 1,1,0,0,0,1,0,0,1.
Digraph: loops at 1 and 3; arrows 1→2 and 2→3; no arrow 1→3.
Composition: R ∘ R = {(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,3),(3,3)}. The new pair (1,3) is exactly the pair transitivity needed.
examples.answer: R is antisymmetric only; it is not reflexive, not symmetric and not transitive. Its matrix is [[1,1,0],[0,0,1],[0,0,1]], R⁻¹ = {(1,1),(2,1),(3,2),(3,3)}, and R ∘ R = {(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,3),(3,3)}.

traps: Treating symmetric and antisymmetric as opposites. Equality on a set is both, and this example is antisymmetric yet not symmetric; a relation can also be neither.
Checking transitivity on only one pair. Every two-step path must have its shortcut; one missing shortcut breaks the property.
Forgetting that reflexivity needs every diagonal pair. A relation can have most diagonal pairs and still fail.
Mixing up a relation from A to B with a relation on A. The matrix is square only for a relation on one set.
Assuming an irreflexive relation is automatically asymmetric. Asymmetry also forbids two-way arrows between distinct elements.

quiz.q: Define a reflexive relation on a set A.
quiz.a: R is reflexive if (a,a) ∈ R for every a ∈ A. In the matrix, the whole main diagonal is 1.

quiz.q: Why is the empty relation on a nonempty set A symmetric and transitive but not reflexive?
quiz.a: There is no pair (a,b) to force a partner (b,a), so symmetry holds. There is no two-step path to force a shortcut, so transitivity holds. Reflexivity needs (a,a) for every a, and A is nonempty, so it fails.

quiz.q: A = {1,2,3}. R = {(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,1)}. Is R reflexive, symmetric and transitive?
quiz.a: Reflexive: yes, all three diagonal pairs are present. Symmetric: yes, (1,2) and (2,1) are both present. Transitive: yes; (1,2) and (2,1) give (1,1), and (2,1) and (1,2) give (2,2).

quiz.q: On a 4-element set, count all relations, all reflexive relations and all symmetric relations.
A relation matrix has all diagonal entries 1, equals its transpose, and satisfies M² ≤ M. Which three properties are guaranteed?
quiz.a: Reflexive from the all-1 diagonal; symmetric from M = Mᵀ; transitive from M² ≤ M.

quiz.q: R = {(1,2),(2,3)} on {1,2,3}. Is R transitive? What one pair makes it transitive?
quiz.a: Not transitive, because (1,2) and (2,3) are in R but (1,3) is not. Adding (1,3) makes it transitive.

beyond: Not for the exam. Relational databases are built from relations with named columns, and query planners reason about joins and keys using these ideas. Graph databases store edges directly and use reachability and composition daily. Type systems and program semantics model behaviour as relations when outputs may be many or none. Search next for relational algebra, binary relations in databases, and transitive closure in graph query languages.
